response.text:
Nice — that's a hands-on way to see it. Here's a live model you can drive yourself: change buses per hour (and the other assumptions) and watch seats available per hour update instantly.

```openui lifecycle=ephemeral id=bus-frequency-seats
root = LearningSurface([model], "Bus frequency → seats available per hour", "Move the sliders; the seats-available number updates as you go.", "ephemeral")
model = Simulation("bus-seats-model", "Hourly seats vs. hourly demand", [
  { id: "busesPerHour", label: "Buses per hour", unit: "buses", min: 1, max: 30, step: 1, value: 8 },
  { id: "seatsPerBus", label: "Seats per bus", unit: "seats", min: 20, max: 80, step: 2, value: 40 },
  { id: "baseRiders", label: "Riders who ride regardless of frequency", unit: "riders", min: 0, max: 600, step: 10, value: 300 },
  { id: "extraRidersPerBus", label: "Extra riders attracted per added bus", unit: "riders", min: 0, max: 40, step: 1, value: 8 }
], [
  { id: "capacity", label: "Seats offered per hour", unit: "seats", expr: "busesPerHour * seatsPerBus", precision: 0 },
  { id: "riders", label: "Riders per hour", unit: "riders", expr: "baseRiders + extraRidersPerBus * busesPerHour", precision: 0 },
  { id: "available", label: "Seats available per hour", unit: "seats", expr: "busesPerHour * seatsPerBus - baseRiders - extraRidersPerBus * busesPerHour", precision: 0, emphasis: true },
  { id: "loadFactor", label: "Load factor", unit: "%", expr: "(baseRiders + extraRidersPerBus * busesPerHour) / (busesPerHour * seatsPerBus) * 100", precision: 1 }
], "ephemeral", "First predict: if you double buses per hour from 8 to 16, will seats available per hour double too? Then move the slider and compare. Note the 'extra riders attracted per added bus' slider — if riders grow as fast as capacity, spare seats can vanish even as service improves. A negative 'seats available' means a shortfall (turn-aways).")
```

A couple of things worth trying once you've played with it: set *extra riders per added bus* to a high value to see how demand can cancel out a service increase, and then set it to 0 to see the pure capacity effect.

Tell me what you find and where the number stops improving — that point is usually where the interesting policy conversation lives.
